title: Understanding Contrastive Learning through Variational Analysis and Neural Network Optimization Perspectives

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to explain why the invariance induced by SimCLR contrastive loss alone cannot guarantee learning good representations, revealing pathological properties of the loss itself. Paper [5] discusses theoretical aspects of contrastive learning but focuses on its superiority over other methods rather than pathological properties. Paper [15] identifies alignment and uniformity as key properties of contrastive loss but does not address pathological invariance or spurious minima. Paper [24] studies the behavior of contrastive loss, including its hardness-aware nature, but does not establish the same pathological invariance issue. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish the same empirical relationship regarding SimCLR's inability to select good minima due to invariance.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses variational analysis to characterize the stationary points and local minima of SimCLR loss, proving the existence of invariant minima unrelated to the data distribution (e.g., uniform hidden distributions). Paper [1] analyzes spurious local minima in neural networks but does not focus on SimCLR or contrastive loss. Paper [4] proves that all local minima are global in deep linear networks but does not address variational analysis of SimCLR loss. Paper [5] provides theoretical analysis of contrastive learning but does not use variational methods to characterize minima. Paper [15] discusses alignment and uniformity but does not analyze stationary points or invariant minima. None of the prior papers employ the same variational analysis mechanism.

### Evaluation
The contribution validates its findings through qualitative and theorem-based results (e.g., Theorem 3.2), showing that SimCLR loss alone is insufficient to select good minima and can lead to trivial invariant distributions. Paper [5] uses theoretical analysis to validate claims about contrastive learning but does not use the same theorem-based evaluation design. Paper [15] empirically analyzes alignment and uniformity but does not employ theorem-based validation. Paper [24] studies the behavior of contrastive loss but does not use qualitative theorem results to validate pathological properties. None of the prior papers use the same evaluation design.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of self-supervised/contrastive representation learning theory. Paper [5] explicitly analyzes contrastive learning in self-supervised settings, as does Paper [15]. Paper [24] also focuses on unsupervised contrastive learning. These papers address the same general application area, even though the specific focus on SimCLR's pathological invariance differs.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to understand the success of contrastive learning by analyzing neural network training dynamics rather than focusing solely on loss minimization. Paper [1] discusses spectral bias and its role in generalization, which indirectly touches on training dynamics but does not explicitly analyze contrastive learning or the role of clustering structures in training dynamics. Paper [2] explores gradient descent's implicit bias but focuses on asymptotic behavior rather than the dynamics during training. Paper [3] introduces the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) to describe training dynamics but does not address contrastive learning or clustering structures. Paper [5] connects NTK evolution to Neural Collapse, which involves clustering structures, but does not analyze contrastive learning specifically. None of the prior papers explicitly address the purpose of analyzing training dynamics to explain contrastive learning success.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses neural kernel methods (single-layer networks) to analyze gradient descent-induced training dynamics and demonstrates that strong data clustering structures influence training dynamics and persist in latent distributions. Paper [3] introduces NTK to describe training dynamics in the infinite-width limit, which is substantively equivalent to the mechanism of using kernel methods to analyze training dynamics. Paper [4] studies feature learning in two-layer networks using kernel methods, focusing on dynamics induced by the first layer, which overlaps with the mechanism of analyzing training dynamics via kernel methods. Paper [5] bridges NTK and Neural Collapse, showing clustering structures emerge during training, which aligns with the mechanism of analyzing clustering structures in training dynamics. Thus, the mechanism is covered.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates its findings through theoretical analysis of single-layer networks and numerical experiments, including t-SNE visualizations on MNIST/CIFAR-10 and SimCLR experiments on CIFAR-10. Paper [3] uses NTK-based theoretical analysis and numerical experiments to validate training dynamics, which matches the evaluation design. Paper [5] employs NTK-based analysis and numerical experiments to study clustering structures, which also aligns with the evaluation design. Paper [4] uses kernel-based theoretical analysis and numerical experiments to validate feature learning dynamics, which matches the evaluation design. The evaluation design is therefore covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of self-supervised/contrastive representation learning theory, specifically focusing on training dynamics. Paper [31] provides a theoretical framework for self-supervised learning, including contrastive learning, which covers the general domain. Paper [32] investigates self-supervised representation learning for functional knowledge transfer, which also falls within the domain of self-supervised learning theory. Paper [33] explores self-supervised learning for video representation tasks, which is a subdomain of self-supervised learning. Thus, the domain is covered.
